title: DeepSeek V4 Flash on a DGX Spark: the real numbers

scenes.narration: DeepSeek V4 Flash runs on the DGX Spark on my desk. It answers at forty-one tokens a second. That number is the whole episode. Here is how I got it, and where it falls apart.
scenes.visual_intent: The episode title and the series tag; the viewer knows this is a measured benchmark, not news.

scenes.narration: First, what we are measuring. DeepSeek V4 Flash is a mixture of experts, a model that wakes up only a slice of itself for each word. The full weights are about one hundred sixty gigabytes in sixteen-bit. That does not fit. So I quantized it, which means storing each weight with fewer bits. At four bits it takes about eighty-five gigabytes of memory. The Spark has one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory, shared between the CPU and the GPU. So it fits, with room for the context.
scenes.visual_intent: The mascot talks while three facts land one at a time: the model is big, quantizing shrinks it, it fits in 128 GB.

scenes.narration: Here is why the Spark can run it at all. The weights load from the NVMe drive into unified memory once. Every new word the model writes needs to read the active experts again. That read goes through the memory bus at two hundred seventy-three gigabytes a second. Flash only wakes about seven billion parameters per word, so each word reads a few gigabytes. Divide the bandwidth by the bytes per word and you get the speed ceiling. The ceiling is about fifty tokens a second. We measured forty-one. The rest is overhead, and we will see where it goes.
scenes.visual_intent: A flow from the drive through unified memory to the GPU; the bandwidth label on the memory-to-GPU arrow is the bottleneck.

scenes.narration: Two commands. The first downloads the four-bit weights from Hugging Face, about eighty-five gigabytes. The second starts llama-server, the HTTP server that ships with llama.cpp. Three flags matter. Dash n g l ninety-nine puts every layer on the GPU. Dash c sets the context window, the amount of conversation the model can see at once. I used thirty-two thousand tokens. Flash attention on keeps the memory for that context small. You'd want the same three flags on any card with enough memory.
scenes.visual_intent: The two shell commands typed out; the three flags that matter are visible when they are spoken.

data.title: serve.sh
data.code:
# pull the Q4 weights (about 85 GB)
hf download unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-GGUF \
  --include "*Q4_K_M*" --local-dir ~/models/dsv4-flash

# serve it on the GPU with a 32k context
llama-server \
  -m ~/models/dsv4-flash/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -c 32768 -fa on \
  --port 8000

scenes.narration: Let me show you the plain run first, with Ollama, because that is what most of you will type. Ollama run, the model name, and verbose. Verbose prints the timing at the end. Watch the last three lines. Prompt eval rate is how fast it reads your question. Eval rate is how fast it writes the answer. That second number is the one you feel. Forty-one point seven tokens a second. A fast reader reads about five words a second, so this is eight times faster than you can read.
scenes.visual_intent: The real terminal session replays: the command, the streamed answer, then the timing block with eval rate highlighted.
on_screen_text: eval rate: the number you feel

scenes.narration: Chapter two. The numbers, all of them, including the ones I did not like.

Here it is on its own. Forty-one point seven tokens a second, generating, with a four-bit model and a thirty-two thousand token context. That is the median of five runs at night with nothing else on the box. The slowest run was thirty-nine. The fastest was forty-three. If your number is within ten percent of this, your setup matches mine.
scenes.visual_intent: One big number, 41.7 tok/s, counts up as it is spoken; the caption names the quantization and context.

scenes.narration: Now the trade-off. I ran the same prompt at three precisions. Four-bit, eight-bit, and eight-bit floating point, which keeps more of the original detail. Four-bit wins on speed at forty-one tokens a second. Eight-bit drops to twenty-eight. FP eight lands at twenty-five, because the kernel, the small program that does the math, is not tuned for this chip yet. Context size costs less than you'd think. Going from eight thousand to thirty-two thousand tokens only cost two or three tokens a second. So the rule is simple. Pick the smallest quantization whose answers you still trust, and do not fear a big context.
scenes.visual_intent: Grouped bars: Q4 is tallest, FP8 shortest; the second series shows the small cost of a bigger context.
on_screen_text: Context costs less than you think

scenes.narration: How does that compare with what you might already own? Three boxes. The Spark, a gaming card, and a Mac Studio with the same memory. The gaming card has thirty-two gigabytes of memory, so the four-bit model does not fit. It is not slow. It simply cannot load. The Mac fits it and generates about thirty-five tokens a second, a bit behind the Spark. The Mac costs more but draws less power. The honest summary: if you already have the Mac, keep it. If you are buying for this model, the Spark is faster per dollar. If you have the gaming card, you want a smaller model, and that is a different episode.
scenes.visual_intent: A table with three machines; the row that matters most (does it fit) shows the gaming card cannot load the model.
on_screen_text: Does it fit? That is the first question

scenes.narration: Chapter three. What it means for the box on your desk.
scenes.visual_intent: Chapter three card: What it means.

scenes.narration: Three things to take away. Fits in one box. A frontier-class open model runs on one machine under your desk, with no cloud bill. Faster than you read. Forty-one tokens a second is eight times reading speed, so the bottleneck is you. Quality costs three points. On my fifty-question spot check the four-bit model got three fewer right than the full model. For coding help and summaries I did not notice. For long math chains I did. That is the trade-off. You decide where it bites.
scenes.visual_intent: Three short lines appear word by word as they are spoken; the last word of each line is in the accent color.

scenes.narration: One line to remember. The number that matters is the one you measured on the box you own. Benchmarks from a vendor slide were made on a machine you do not have, with a prompt you will never type. Run it yourself. It takes one evening.
scenes.visual_intent: The one sentence to remember, large, with the attribution under it.

scenes.narration: This is the box. It is the size of a thick paperback. It sat on my desk for the whole week of runs. The fan is quiet until the model loads, then you hear it. I kept the window open in the script so you can see the same numbers scroll past.
scenes.visual_intent: The Spark on the desk with the terminal on the screen behind it; the viewer sees the physical size of the machine.
